quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on construction notation, count systems, crimp, wastage and B-grade as they are used in fabric yarn costing.

questions.q: In the construction 20×20/60×60, 63″, what do the four numbers before the width mean?
options: Warp count × weft count / ends per inch × picks per inch
Ends per inch × picks per inch / warp count × weft count
Warp count × ends per inch / weft count × picks per inch
Warp weight × weft weight / warp price × weft price
questions.explain: The lecture writes constructions as warp × weft / ends × picks, width: Ne 20 warp, Ne 20 weft, 60 ends and 60 picks per inch, 63 inches wide.

questions.q: What does an English cotton count (Ne) of 20 mean?
options: 20 hanks of 840 yd weigh one pound
questions.explain: Ne is an indirect system: the number of 840 yd hanks per pound. Ne 20 means 16,800 yd weigh 1 lb; the higher the count, the finer the yarn.

questions.q: Denier is a direct count system used mainly for filament yarns.
questions.explain: Denier is the weight in grams of 9,000 m of yarn, so a higher denier means a heavier, coarser yarn. The lecture converts it with denier = 5,315 ÷ Ne.

questions.q: Why is the warp weight per yard of fabric greater than the weight of one yard of all the ends?
options: Because of crimp (contraction) and wastage, and because B-grade fabric must still be paid for
Because the price per 10 lb is used
questions.explain: 0.2250 lb of ends becomes 0.2568 lb per yard of fabric once the yarn is grossed up by (1 + crimp + wastage) and divided by (1 − B-grade).

questions.q: What is warp contraction (crimp)?
options: The shrinkage of fabric after washing
The extra yarn length needed because the warp bends over and under the picks, so a yard of fabric holds more than a yard of warp
The loss of ends during sizing
The reduction in width on the loom
questions.explain: Crimp means a yard of fabric contains, for example, 1.10 yd of warp yarn when contraction is 10 %. Width reduction is weft contraction's cousin, not warp crimp.

questions.q: What does the B-grade adjustment in the yarn cost do?
options: Reduces the yarn weight because B-grade is lighter
Increases the yarn charged to each A-grade yard, because the yarn in rejected fabric was still bought
questions.explain: Dividing by (1 − B-grade) spreads the yarn used in B-grade cloth over the A-grade yards that are sold at full price.

questions.q: Yarn is normally the biggest single cost in a metre of grey fabric.
questions.explain: The lecture says so directly: multiply the yarn weight by its price and you have the biggest single cost of the fabric, Rs 27.79 per metre here.

questions.q: Yarn prices in the lecture's sheet are quoted per…
questions.explain: Warp and weft prices are entered as Rs per 10 lb (Rs 500 here, i.e. Rs 50 per lb). Using the figure as a per-lb price would overstate the cost tenfold.

questions.q: Which of these is wastage, as distinct from crimp?
options: Yarn length consumed by bending in the cloth
Yarn lost in warping, sizing, knotting and loom waste that never becomes fabric
questions.explain: Wastage is yarn bought but lost in the process; crimp is yarn that is in the fabric but hidden in its bends. Both raise yarn needed per yard and are added together in the lecture's formula.

questions.q: A yard of fabric is converted to a metre by…
questions.explain: A metre is 1.0936 yd, so the cost per metre is the cost per yard × 1.0936 (Rs 25.41 → Rs 27.79). Dividing would make the metre cheaper than the yard.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The warp and weft weight formulas, the denier conversion, and how each input moves the yarn cost per metre.

questions.q: Warp weight per yard of fabric (lb) before the B-grade adjustment is…
options: ends per inch × (1 + crimp + wastage) ÷ (840 × Ne)
questions.explain: Total ends (not ends per inch) × grossing factor ÷ yards per pound. 3,780 × 1.13 ÷ 16,800 = 0.2543 lb, then ÷ 0.99 for B-grade gives 0.2568.

questions.q: Weft weight per yard of fabric uses picks per inch × 36 × width in yards. What does picks × 36 × width give?
options: The total yards of weft yarn in one yard of fabric before crimp
questions.explain: 60 picks per inch × 36 in = 2,160 picks per yard, each 1.75 yd long = 3,780 yd of weft per yard of fabric, before crimp and wastage.

questions.q: The length of 1 lb of Ne 20 yarn is…
questions.explain: 840 × 20 = 16,800 yd per lb. Dividing instead gives a tiny length and a weight 400 times too large.

questions.q: If the warp count changes from Ne 20 to Ne 40 with the same ends per inch, the warp weight per yard…
questions.explain: Weight is inversely proportional to Ne: 840 × 40 = 33,600 yd per lb, so the same length of yarn weighs half as much.

questions.q: Raising the picks per inch from 60 to 72 raises the weft weight per yard by 20 % but leaves the warp weight unchanged.
questions.explain: Weft weight is proportional to picks per inch (72 ÷ 60 = 1.2); the warp weight depends on ends, not picks.

questions.q: What is the effect on yarn cost per metre of raising the B-grade allowance from 1 % to 2 %?
options: Cost rises by about 1 % (÷ 0.98 instead of ÷ 0.99)
Cost is unchanged because B-grade is sold
questions.explain: The divisor changes from 0.99 to 0.98, raising both warp and weft weight by a factor of 0.99 ÷ 0.98 ≈ 1.0102, about 1 %.

questions.q: Denier in terms of Ne is…
questions.explain: The two systems are inverse to each other, and the constant 5,315 links them: Ne 30 ≈ 177 denier, Ne 20 ≈ 266 denier.

questions.q: Cost per yard of warp is found by…
options: warp weight per yard (lb) × price per 10 lb
warp weight per yard (lb) × price per 10 lb ÷ 10
warp weight per yard (lb) ÷ price per 10 lb
questions.explain: 0.2568 lb × Rs 500 per 10 lb ÷ 10 = 0.2568 × Rs 50 = Rs 12.84 per yard. Forgetting the ÷ 10 gives Rs 128, ten times too high.

questions.q: If fabric width rises from 63″ to 72″ at the same ends and picks per inch, which yarn weights per yard change?
options: Both warp and weft, in proportion to width
questions.explain: Total ends = ends per inch × width, and weft length = picks × 36 × width; both scale by 72 ÷ 63. A wider cloth has more ends and longer picks.

questions.q: Warp and weft contraction are always equal, so one crimp figure is enough.
questions.explain: The sheet has separate inputs; a 60 × 60 square cloth may still have 10 % warp and 5 % weft contraction, because warp is held under tension on the loom.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Compute ends, yarn lengths, warp and weft weights and the yarn cost per yard and per metre, with the lecture's inputs and a few new ones.

questions.q: A fabric has 60 ends per inch and is 63 inches wide. How many total ends does it have?
questions.explain: 60 × 63 = 3,780 ends across the width.

questions.q: How many yards of Ne 20 cotton yarn weigh one pound?
questions.explain: 840 yd per hank × 20 hanks per lb = 16,800 yd per lb.

questions.q: 3,780 ends of Ne 20 yarn (16,800 yd per lb) run through one yard of fabric. What is the weight of one yard of all the ends, in lb, before crimp and wastage (four decimals)?
questions.explain: 3,780 yd of yarn ÷ 16,800 yd per lb = 0.2250 lb.

questions.q: Using 0.2250 lb of ends per yard, warp contraction 10 %, warp wastage 3 % and B-grade 1 %, find the warp weight per yard of fabric in lb (four decimals).
questions.explain: 0.2250 × 1.13 ÷ 0.99 = 0.2568 lb per yard, as in the sheet.

questions.q: A fabric has 60 picks per inch and is 1.75 yd wide. How many yards of weft yarn are in one yard of fabric, before crimp and wastage?
questions.explain: 60 × 36 = 2,160 picks per yard of fabric, each 1.75 yd long: 2,160 × 1.75 = 3,780 yd.

questions.q: Weft is Ne 20 (16,800 yd per lb), 3,780 yd of weft per yard of fabric, weft contraction 5 %, weft wastage 5 %, B-grade 1 %. Find the weft weight per yard of fabric in lb (four decimals).
questions.explain: 0.2250 × 1.10 ÷ 0.99 = 0.2500 lb per yard (the lecture's sheet shows 0.2514 with its own wastage input).

questions.q: Warp weight is 0.2568 lb per yard and warp yarn costs Rs 500 per 10 lb. What is the warp cost per yard (to the nearest paisa)?
questions.explain: Rs 500 per 10 lb = Rs 50 per lb; 0.2568 × 50 = Rs 12.84 per yard.

questions.q: Warp cost is Rs 12.84 and weft cost Rs 12.57 per yard. What is the yarn cost per metre (1 m = 1.0936 yd), to the nearest paisa?
questions.explain: Rs 25.41 per yard × 1.0936 = Rs 27.79 per metre.

questions.q: What is the denier equivalent of Ne 30 (denier = 5,315 ÷ Ne), to the nearest whole number?
The same fabric is woven with Ne 40 warp instead of Ne 20, all else equal. What is the new warp weight per yard?
questions.explain: Doubling the count halves the weight: 0.2568 ÷ 2 = 0.1284 lb. Doubling to 0.5136 is the common reversal error.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Costing-office situations: checking a quotation, choosing between constructions and spotting the input that has gone wrong.

questions.q: A junior costs a 20×20/60×60 fabric and gets Rs 128.40 per yard of warp. The weight is 0.2568 lb. What has happened?
options: The Rs 500 per 10 lb price was applied per lb
Ends were counted per inch only
questions.explain: 0.2568 × 500 = 128.4; the price should have been divided by 10 to give Rs 50 per lb and Rs 12.84 per yard.

questions.q: A buyer asks for the same construction at 72″ instead of 63″. The merchandiser quotes the same yarn cost per metre. Is that right?
options: Yes, yarn per metre depends only on counts
No, both warp and weft yarn rise by 72 ÷ 63, so yarn cost rises about 14 %
questions.explain: More ends across the width and longer picks: both weights scale with width. Rs 27.79 becomes about Rs 31.76 per metre.

questions.q: Warp yarn is offered at Rs 480 per 10 lb from one spinner and Rs 500 from another whose yarn gives 1 % less wastage. For the lecture's fabric (warp 0.2568 lb per yard at 3 % wastage), which is cheaper per yard?
options: Rs 480 spinner, by about Rs 0.40 per yard
Rs 500 spinner, by about Rs 0.40 per yard
Rs 500 spinner, by about Rs 2 per yard
questions.explain: Rs 480: 0.2568 × 48 = Rs 12.33. Rs 500 with 2 % wastage: 0.225 × 1.12 ÷ 0.99 × 50 = Rs 12.73. The 4 % price cut beats a 1-point wastage saving.

questions.q: If a mill's B-grade rises from 1 % to 5 %, its yarn cost per A-grade metre rises by roughly 4 %.
questions.explain: The divisor falls from 0.99 to 0.95: 0.99 ÷ 0.95 = 1.042, about 4 % more yarn charged to each saleable metre.

questions.q: A customer wants a lighter fabric at the same price. Which change reduces yarn cost most for a 20×20/60×60 cloth?
questions.explain: Picks down 20 % cuts weft cost by 20 % (about Rs 2.5 per yard). One inch of width is 1.6 %; the B-grade and wastage changes are each under 1 %.

questions.q: A filament supplier quotes 150 denier polyester. For the yarn-weight formula built on Ne, what should the costing clerk do?
questions.explain: Denier and Ne are inverse systems linked by 5,315. Using 150 as Ne would make the yarn appear four times lighter than it is.

questions.q: The costing sheet shows weft weight per yard higher than warp weight even though counts and settings are equal. What is the likely reason?
options: An arithmetic error, since they must be equal
Higher weft wastage or contraction inputs than warp
questions.explain: With 60 × 60 and both Ne 20 the base weights are both 0.2250 lb; any difference comes from the contraction and wastage inputs for each direction.

questions.q: Yarn prices rise 10 % the day after a fabric quotation at Rs 27.79 yarn cost per metre is sent. What is the new yarn cost per metre?
questions.explain: Yarn cost is directly proportional to yarn price: Rs 27.79 × 1.10 = Rs 30.57 per metre. A quotation must carry a validity period for this reason.

questions.q: Quoting yarn cost per yard to a buyer who asked for a price per metre understates the cost by about 9 %.
questions.explain: A metre is 9.36 % longer than a yard: Rs 25.41 per yard against Rs 27.79 per metre. Always confirm the unit of length.

questions.q: Which input error would most inflate the yarn cost of a 20×20/60×60, 63″ fabric?
options: Entering width as 63 yd instead of 1.75 yd
Entering warp crimp as 11 % instead of 10 %
Entering weft price as Rs 505 instead of Rs 500
questions.explain: Width in yards feeds the weft length; 63 instead of 1.75 multiplies weft weight by 36. The other errors change the cost by about 1 % each.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step problems across the lecture: rebuilding the sheet from the inputs, reversing the formulas and catching the classic slips.

questions.q: A 30×30/80×70 fabric is 48″ wide. Warp Ne 30, 80 ends per inch, crimp 8 %, wastage 2 %, B-grade 1 %. Find the warp weight per yard of fabric in lb (four decimals).
The same fabric: weft Ne 30, 70 picks per inch, width 48″ (1.3333 yd), weft crimp 4 %, wastage 3 %, B-grade 1 %. Find the weft weight per yard in lb (four decimals).
Warp 0.1693 lb and weft 0.1441 lb per yard; both yarns cost Rs 620 per 10 lb. What is the yarn cost per metre (1 m = 1.0936 yd), to the nearest paisa?
questions.explain: 0.3134 lb × Rs 62 per lb = Rs 19.43 per yard; × 1.0936 = Rs 21.25 per metre.

questions.q: A costing shows warp weight per yard of 0.2568 lb for 3,780 ends of Ne 20 with 10 % crimp, 3 % wastage, 1 % B-grade. A colleague multiplies 1.10 × 1.03 ÷ 0.99 instead of adding crimp and wastage. How different is the result?
questions.explain: 1.10 × 1.03 = 1.133 against 1 + 0.10 + 0.03 = 1.13. The lecture adds them; multiplying is a different convention and gives 0.2575 lb, a negligible but real difference.

questions.q: A yard of fabric contains 0.2568 lb of warp yarn at Ne 20. Taking 16,800 yd per lb, how many yards of warp yarn is that?
questions.explain: 0.2568 × 16,800 = 4,314 yd, against 3,780 yd of fabric-length ends: the extra 534 yd is crimp, wastage and B-grade allowance.

questions.q: To halve the weft cost per yard of a 20×20/60×60 fabric while keeping 60 picks, the weft count should become…
questions.explain: Weight is inversely proportional to Ne, so Ne 40 halves it. Ne 10 doubles it. Halving width also halves it but changes the product.

questions.q: For a square construction (same count, ends and picks), the warp and weft base weights per yard before crimp are equal because 36 × width in yards equals the width in inches.
questions.explain: Total ends = EPI × width in inches; weft length = PPI × 36 × width in yards = PPI × width in inches. With EPI = PPI and equal counts the base weights match (0.2250 lb each here).

questions.q: Yarn cost per metre is Rs 27.79 at a B-grade of 1 %. What would it be at a B-grade of 3 % with all other inputs unchanged (to the nearest paisa)?
questions.explain: Both weights are divided by (1 − B): Rs 27.79 × 0.99 ÷ 0.97 = Rs 28.36 per metre.

questions.q: A merchandiser argues that B-grade should not raise the yarn cost because B-grade cloth is also sold. Which is the better view, following Lectures 18 and 19?
options: Charge all yarn to A-grade yards, then bring in the B-grade sale as a small credit in the production cost
Deduct the B-grade percentage from the yarn cost
questions.explain: The lecture grosses up yarn by ÷ (1 − B) and the next lecture credits the B-grade proceeds per metre. Both effects are then shown honestly rather than netted off in the yarn weight.

questions.q: What Ne is equivalent to 100 denier (denier = 5,315 ÷ Ne), to one decimal place?
questions.explain: Ne = 5,315 ÷ 100 = 53.15, about Ne 53. A finer (lower) denier gives a higher Ne.
